cases.abstract: An attention-free architecture can remain competitive with hierarchical vision Transformers when convolutional design and training are updated together. We develop ConvNeXt by progressively reworking ResNet with design choices associated with Transformers, while retaining a convolutional architecture. A fixed, modernized training recipe allows architectural changes to be assessed after the initial improvement due to training, and computational cost is kept approximately aligned with Swin models. The resulting blocks combine large depthwise kernels with expanded pointwise channel transformations, fewer activations, and layer normalization. Evaluations cover ImageNet classification, COCO detection and instance segmentation, and ADE20K semantic segmentation. At 384 x 384 resolution, ImageNet-1K-trained ConvNeXt-B reaches 85.1% top-1 accuracy versus Swin-B's 84.5%, while V100 inference throughput rises from 85.1 to 95.7 images per second. ImageNet-22K pretraining supports further scaling, with ConvNeXt-XL reaching 87.8% after fine-tuning at the same resolution. Downstream comparisons are also competitive with similarly sized Swin backbones. These results establish a convolutional alternative for the evaluated recognition tasks without shifted-window attention or relative position biases.
cases.methods: The central block separates spatial mixing from channel mixing. A 7 x 7 depthwise convolution operates before two pointwise convolutions that expand the channel dimension fourfold and then restore it. Placing the spatial operator at the narrower input width keeps large receptive fields affordable, while the pointwise layers supply channel capacity. Only one GELU activation and one layer normalization remain within each residual block. Separate stride-two convolutions handle transitions between stages; adding them without extra normalization at resolution changes caused training to diverge. This architecture is developed through sequential modifications of a ResNet baseline trained for 300 epochs with AdamW, augmentation, and regularization. The same recipe and hyperparameters are retained across the modernization sequence, FLOPs are controlled approximately, and reported small-model accuracies average three training seeds. The sequence therefore evaluates an accumulated design rather than independently isolating every component's effect.
cases.results: At 384 x 384 resolution, ImageNet-1K-trained ConvNeXt-B improves both accuracy and measured inference throughput over Swin-B: 85.1% versus 84.5% top-1, and 95.7 versus 85.1 images per second on V100. Its computational cost is also slightly lower, at 45.0 versus 47.1 GFLOPs. This is a favorable comparison with a similarly sized Transformer, not the highest accuracy among every tested model: EfficientNetV2-L reaches 85.7%, using 480 x 480 inputs and 53.0 GFLOPs. Downstream fine-tuning shows that the benefit extends beyond classification. With ImageNet-22K pretraining and Cascade Mask R-CNN, ConvNeXt-B obtains 54.0 box AP and 46.9 mask AP, compared with Swin-B's 53.0 and 45.8. With the same pretraining, UperNet, 640 x 640 crops, and multi-scale testing, ADE20K mIoU is 53.1 versus 51.7. These comparisons support competitive convolutional features across the evaluated recognition tasks without conflating classification throughput, detection accuracy, and segmentation quality.
cases.notes: The modernization narrative ends at 82.0%, whereas the main evaluation lists 82.1% for ConvNeXt-T; no reconciliation is assumed. Sequential modifications do not independently identify all component effects. Throughput figures used here are V100 classification measurements, not COCO FPS measured on A100.

cases.abstract: Photographic scene reconstruction must reconcile the cost of fitting a radiance field with the cost of rendering it for interactive exploration. We represent static scenes with optimized anisotropic 3D Gaussians, initialized from sparse structure-from-motion points and assigned spherical harmonic coefficients for directional color. Geometry and appearance are learned jointly while cloning, splitting, and pruning adapt the representation to missing detail and oversized primitives. A differentiable tile renderer sorts splats for approximate visibility-aware blending and propagates gradients without a fixed limit on contributors. Across 13 real scenes and synthetic bounded scenes, the method combines rapid rendering with progressively improved reconstruction. At 30,000 iterations, real-dataset averages reach 134-154 frames per second at native image resolutions on an A6000, after approximately 27-42 minutes of training. Quality is competitive with Mip-NeRF360, although on its dataset Gaussian splatting improves SSIM and LPIPS while retaining lower PSNR. The explicit representation therefore changes the practical quality-speed tradeoff rather than winning every image metric. Its costs include substantially larger stored models than neural radiance fields, artifacts in poorly observed regions, and occasional popping.
cases.methods: To make an explicit radiance field trainable as well as fast to display, the renderer groups projected Gaussians into 16 x 16 pixel tiles. Each overlapping Gaussian receives a key combining tile identity and view-space depth, so a single GPU radix sort supplies ordered lists for all tiles. Pixels accumulate color and opacity from front to back, stopping when opacity saturates rather than after a fixed number of contributors. The backward pass traverses the same lists in reverse and reconstructs intermediate blending information from stored final accumulation values, avoiding variable-length lists per pixel while allowing every contributing splat to receive gradients. This supports scenes with varying depth complexity without imposing an arbitrary gradient cutoff. Rendering losses jointly update Gaussian geometry, opacity, and spherical harmonic color, interleaved with gradient-guided cloning and splitting. Ordering is shared within tiles rather than recomputed per pixel, so blending remains approximate.
cases.results: On the Mip-NeRF360 dataset, Gaussian splatting at 30,000 iterations raises SSIM from 0.792 to 0.815 and lowers LPIPS from 0.237 to 0.214 relative to Mip-NeRF360, but PSNR falls from 27.69 to 27.21 dB. The quality advantage is therefore metric-dependent. The Gaussian model renders at 134 frames per second on an A6000 after an average 41 minutes 33 seconds of optimization, while its stored parameters occupy 734 MB versus Mip-NeRF360's 8.6 MB. Early stopping introduces another tradeoff: on Tanks & Temples, PSNR rises from 21.20 at 7,000 iterations to 23.14 at 30,000, while rendering drops from 197 to 154 frames per second. In a separate 30,000-iteration Truck ablation, limiting gradients to ten splats reduces PSNR from 24.81 to 13.84 dB, showing that this gradient shortcut can seriously compromise fitting. High frame rates also coexist with occasional popping and artifacts in regions poorly covered by training views.
cases.notes: Mip-NeRF360's quality scores on its own dataset were adopted from its publication; other main-table quality scores were obtained in the authors' runs. The reported 48-hour baseline training figure aggregates four A100 GPUs used for 12 hours, not an A6000 wall-clock measurement, so it is not used for a matched-hardware speedup. Ablation inputs were manually downsampled separately. Memory numbers in Results describe stored parameters, not peak training memory; the latter can exceed 20 GB for large scenes.
